title: Quadratic Expressions
description: Expanding double brackets and factorising quadratic expressions — an introduction to quadratics.

notes.heading: What is a Quadratic Expression?
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A quadratic expression is an algebraic expression in which the highest power of the variable is $2$. In one variable it has the form
$$ax^2 + bx + c$$
where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are numbers and $a \neq 0$.

🔑 How it works
• $a$ is the coefficient of $x^2$.
• $b$ is the coefficient of $x$.
• $c$ is the constant term.
• $b$ or $c$ can be zero — the expression is still quadratic as long as $a \neq 0$.

💡 Worked Example
State the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$ for each expression.

• $x^2 + 7x + 12$: $a = 1$, $b = 7$, $c = 12$
• $3x^2 - 5x + 2$: $a = 3$, $b = -5$, $c = 2$
• $x^2 - 9$: $a = 1$, $b = 0$, $c = -9$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The power of $2$ is what makes an expression quadratic.
• A coefficient belongs to the term that follows it, including its sign.
• Quadratic expressions are built by expanding double brackets, and broken back down by factorising.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking every quadratic must have three terms. $x^2 - 9$ and $x^2 + 6x$ are both quadratic even though one term is missing — the missing coefficient is simply $0$.

notes.heading: Expanding Double Brackets
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Expanding double brackets means multiplying out a product such as $(x + 3)(x + 5)$ so that no brackets remain. Every term in the first bracket must be multiplied by every term in the second bracket.

🔑 How it works
The four products are often remembered as FOIL — First, Outside, Inside, Last:
• First: $x \times x = x^2$
• Outside: $x \times 5 = 5x$
• Inside: $3 \times x = 3x$
• Last: $3 \times 5 = 15$

Then collect the like terms $5x + 3x$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Expand $(x + 3)(x + 5)$.
$$(x + 3)(x + 5) = x^2 + 5x + 3x + 15 = x^2 + 8x + 15$$

💡 Worked Example 2
Expand $(2x + 3)(x + 4)$.
$$(2x + 3)(x + 4) = 2x^2 + 8x + 3x + 12 = 2x^2 + 11x + 12$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• There are always four products before simplifying; two of them usually combine into one $x$ term.
• The result of expanding two linear brackets is a quadratic expression.
• Multiply coefficients and add powers of the variable: $2x \times x = 2x^2$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Multiplying only the First and Last terms and writing $(x + 3)(x + 5) = x^2 + 15$. The Outside and Inside products $5x$ and $3x$ must not be dropped.

✅ Check
Substitute a simple value such as $x = 1$: $(1 + 3)(1 + 5) = 4 \times 6 = 24$, and $1 + 8 + 15 = 24$. Both sides agree.

notes.heading: Expanding Brackets with Negative Terms
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The same four-product method applies when one or both brackets contain negative terms — but the sign rules for multiplication must be applied to every product.

🔑 How it works
• Positive $\times$ positive = positive
• Positive $\times$ negative = negative
• Negative $\times$ negative = positive

Keep the sign attached to each term as you multiply.

💡 Worked Example 1
Expand $(x - 4)(x + 2)$.
• First: $x \times x = x^2$
• Outside: $x \times 2 = 2x$
• Inside: $-4 \times x = -4x$
• Last: $-4 \times 2 = -8$
$$(x - 4)(x + 2) = x^2 + 2x - 4x - 8 = x^2 - 2x - 8$$

💡 Worked Example 2
Expand $(x - 3)(x - 5)$.
$$(x - 3)(x - 5) = x^2 - 5x - 3x + 15 = x^2 - 8x + 15$$
The Last product is positive because $-3 \times -5 = 15$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Write the sign in front of each term before multiplying.
• Two negative brackets give a positive constant term.
• One negative bracket gives a negative constant term.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Losing the sign on the Last product, e.g. writing $(x - 3)(x - 5) = x^2 - 8x - 15$. Remember that $-3 \times -5 = +15$, not $-15$.

notes.heading: Squaring a Bracket and the Difference of Two Squares
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• Squaring a bracket: $(x + a)^2$ means $(x + a)(x + a)$, which expands to $x^2 + 2ax + a^2$.
• Difference of two squares: $(x + a)(x - a)$ expands to $x^2 - a^2$.

🔑 How it works
For a square, the Outside and Inside products are identical, so they double:
$$(x + a)^2 = x^2 + ax + ax + a^2 = x^2 + 2ax + a^2$$

For $(x + a)(x - a)$ the middle terms cancel:
$$(x + a)(x - a) = x^2 - ax + ax - a^2 = x^2 - a^2$$

💡 Worked Example 1
Expand $(x + 6)^2$.
$$(x + 6)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 6x + 36 = x^2 + 12x + 36$$

💡 Worked Example 2
Expand $(x + 5)(x - 5)$.
$$(x + 5)(x - 5) = x^2 - 5x + 5x - 25 = x^2 - 25$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $(x + a)^2$ always produces three terms, including the middle term $2ax$.
• $(x + a)(x - a)$ produces only two terms — the $x$ terms cancel.
• These two patterns save time and appear constantly when factorising.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $(x + 6)^2 = x^2 + 36$. Squaring each term separately misses the middle term; the correct expansion is $x^2 + 12x + 36$.

notes.heading: Factorising Quadratics: $x^2 + bx + c$
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Factorising a quadratic is the reverse of expanding double brackets: the expression $x^2 + bx + c$ is rewritten as a product $(x + p)(x + q)$.

🔑 How it works
Expanding $(x + p)(x + q)$ gives $x^2 + (p + q)x + pq$. So to factorise $x^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers $p$ and $q$ that:
• multiply to give the constant term $c$, and
• add to give the coefficient $b$.

List the factor pairs of $c$ and test their sums.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $x^2 + 7x + 12$.

Factor pairs of $12$: $1 \times 12$, $2 \times 6$, $3 \times 4$.
Their sums: $13$, $8$, $7$. The pair $3$ and $4$ adds to $7$.
$$x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)$$

✅ Check
Expand: $(x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 4x + 3x + 12 = x^2 + 7x + 12$. Correct.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The two numbers must satisfy BOTH conditions: product $= c$ and sum $= b$.
• Start by listing factor pairs of the constant term.
• Always check by expanding your brackets.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Choosing a pair that multiplies to $c$ but does not add to $b$. For $x^2 + 7x + 12$, the pair $2$ and $6$ multiplies to $12$ but adds to $8$, so $(x + 2)(x + 6)$ is wrong.

notes.heading: Factorising Quadratics with Negative Coefficients
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When $b$ or $c$ is negative, the factor pair must include negative numbers. The signs of $b$ and $c$ tell you the signs inside the brackets.

🔑 How it works
• If $c$ is positive, both numbers have the SAME sign as $b$.
• If $c$ is negative, the two numbers have OPPOSITE signs, and the number with the larger size takes the sign of $b$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Factorise $x^2 - 2x - 15$.

$c = -15$ is negative, so the pair has opposite signs. Pairs multiplying to $-15$: $-1, 15$; $1, -15$; $-3, 5$; $3, -5$.
Sums: $14$, $-14$, $2$, $-2$. The pair $3$ and $-5$ adds to $-2$.
$$x^2 - 2x - 15 = (x + 3)(x - 5)$$

💡 Worked Example 2
Factorise $x^2 - 8x + 15$.

$c = 15$ is positive and $b = -8$ is negative, so both numbers are negative. The pair $-3$ and $-5$ multiplies to $15$ and adds to $-8$.
$$x^2 - 8x + 15 = (x - 3)(x - 5)$$

✅ Check
Expand $(x + 3)(x - 5) = x^2 - 5x + 3x - 15 = x^2 - 2x - 15$. Correct.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Product negative $\Rightarrow$ opposite signs; product positive $\Rightarrow$ same signs.
• Check both conditions before writing the brackets.
• Expanding your answer is the fastest way to catch a sign error.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping the signs, e.g. writing $x^2 - 2x - 15 = (x - 3)(x + 5)$. Expanding gives $x^2 + 2x - 15$ — the sign of the middle term is wrong.

notes.heading: Special Factorising Cases and Common Mistakes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Some quadratics factorise using shortcuts instead of the full factor-pair method:
• Difference of two squares: $x^2 - a^2 = (x + a)(x - a)$
• No constant term: take out $x$ as a common factor
• Perfect square: $x^2 + 2ax + a^2 = (x + a)^2$

🔑 How it works
Spot the pattern first, then apply the matching rule.

💡 Worked Example 1 — difference of two squares
Factorise $x^2 - 9$.

Since $9 = 3^2$:
$$x^2 - 9 = (x + 3)(x - 3)$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — common factor only
Factorise $x^2 + 6x$.

Both terms contain $x$:
$$x^2 + 6x = x(x + 6)$$

💡 Worked Example 3 — perfect square
Factorise $x^2 + 10x + 25$.

The pair $5$ and $5$ multiplies to $25$ and adds to $10$:
$$x^2 + 10x + 25 = (x + 5)^2$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A quadratic with no constant term always has $x$ as a common factor.
• $x^2 - a^2$ factorises, but $x^2 + a^2$ does not factorise over whole numbers.
• Expanding and factorising are inverse operations — one always checks the other.

⚠️ Common Mistakes — summary
• $(x + a)^2 = x^2 + a^2$ — wrong; the middle term $2ax$ is missing.
• Choosing a factor pair that multiplies to $c$ but does not add to $b$.
• Putting the wrong sign in each bracket when $c$ is negative.
• Forgetting that $x^2 - 9$ factorises as $(x + 3)(x - 3)$, not $(x - 3)^2$.

✅ Check
Whatever you factorise, expand the result and compare it with the original expression term by term.

flashcards.definition: An algebraic expression whose highest power of the variable is $2$, of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$ with $a \neq 0$.
The number multiplying a variable or power of a variable, including its sign.
The term in an expression that contains no variable.
Multiplying every term in the first bracket by every term in the second bracket, then collecting like terms.
A reminder of the four products when expanding double brackets: First, Outside, Inside, Last.
$(x + a)^2 = (x + a)(x + a) = x^2 + 2ax + a^2$; the middle term must not be forgotten.
The pattern $x^2 - a^2 = (x + a)(x - a)$, where the middle terms cancel when expanded.
Rewriting $x^2 + bx + c$ as a product of two brackets $(x + p)(x + q)$ — the reverse of expanding.
To factorise $x^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$.
If $c$ is positive both bracket signs match the sign of $b$; if $c$ is negative the brackets have opposite signs.
A quadratic that factorises into one bracket squared, $x^2 + 2ax + a^2 = (x + a)^2$.
Verifying a factorisation by expanding the brackets and comparing with the original expression.

questions.explanation: The four products are $x^2$, $5x$, $2x$ and $10$. Collecting like terms gives $x^2 + 7x + 10$.
Expanding gives $x^2 + 4x + 3x + 12$, and $4x + 3x = 7x$, so the answer is $x^2 + 7x + 12$.
The products are $x^2$, $6x$, $-2x$ and $-12$. Since $6x - 2x = 4x$, the result is $x^2 + 4x - 12$.
The products are $x^2$, $-5x$, $-3x$ and $+15$ because $-3 \times -5 = 15$. So $(x - 3)(x - 5) = x^2 - 8x + 15$.
This is a difference of two squares: the middle terms $-7x$ and $+7x$ cancel, leaving $x^2 - 49$.
$(x + 4)^2 = (x + 4)(x + 4) = x^2 + 4x + 4x + 16 = x^2 + 8x + 16$. Squaring each term alone misses the middle term.
The products are $2x^2$, $6x$, $x$ and $3$. Since $6x + x = 7x$, the result is $2x^2 + 7x + 3$.
The pair $4$ and $5$ multiplies to $20$ and adds to $9$, so $x^2 + 9x + 20 = (x + 4)(x + 5)$. The pair $2$ and $10$ adds to $12$, not $9$.
The pair $2$ and $5$ multiplies to $10$ and adds to $7$, giving $(x + 2)(x + 5)$. Expanding $(x - 2)(x - 5)$ would give $-7x$.
A pair multiplying to $-12$ and adding to $-1$ is $-4$ and $3$, so $x^2 - x - 12 = (x - 4)(x + 3)$. The swapped signs give $x^2 + x - 12$.
Since $c = 18$ is positive and $b = -9$ is negative, both numbers are negative: $-3$ and $-6$ multiply to $18$ and add to $-9$.
This is a difference of two squares with $a = 4$: $x^2 - 16 = (x + 4)(x - 4)$. Expanding $(x - 4)^2$ would give $x^2 - 8x + 16$.
The pair $6$ and $-4$ multiplies to $-24$ and adds to $2$, so $x^2 + 2x - 24 = (x + 6)(x - 4)$. The larger number takes the sign of $b$.
The pair $5$ and $5$ multiplies to $25$ and adds to $10$, so this is the perfect square $(x + 5)^2$.

questions.stem: Which pair of numbers multiplies to $-18$ and adds to $-7$?
questions.explanation: The product $-18$ requires opposite signs, and $-9 + 2 = -7$. The pair $9$ and $-2$ adds to $+7$, and $-3$ and $6$ adds to $+3$.
The products are $x^2$, $6x$, $4x$ and $24$, and $6x + 4x = 10x$, so the expansion is $x^2 + 10x + 24$.
Since $36 = 6^2$ this is a difference of two squares: $x^2 - 36 = (x + 6)(x - 6)$. Expanding $(x - 6)^2$ would give a middle term $-12x$.

questions.stem: Which pair of numbers multiplies to $-20$ and adds to $1$?
questions.explanation: The negative product means opposite signs, and $5 + (-4) = 1$ with $5 \times (-4) = -20$. The pair $-5$ and $4$ adds to $-1$ instead.
The products are $x^2$, $-2x$, $5x$ and $-10$. Since $5x - 2x = 3x$, the result is $x^2 + 3x - 10$; the constant is negative because $5 \times (-2) = -10$.
The middle terms $-9x$ and $+9x$ cancel, leaving the difference of two squares $x^2 - 81$.
$(x + 7)^2 = (x + 7)(x + 7) = x^2 + 7x + 7x + 49 = x^2 + 14x + 49$. Squaring each term alone misses the middle term $14x$.
The pair $3$ and $5$ multiplies to $15$ and adds to $8$, so $x^2 + 8x + 15 = (x + 3)(x + 5)$. The pair $1$ and $15$ adds to $16$, not $8$.
Since $c = 12$ is positive and $b = -7$ is negative, both numbers are negative: $-3$ and $-4$ multiply to $12$ and add to $-7$.
The pair $6$ and $6$ multiplies to $36$ and adds to $12$, so this is the perfect square $(x + 6)^2$.
The products are $3x^2$, $15x$, $2x$ and $10$. Since $15x + 2x = 17x$, the result is $3x^2 + 17x + 10$.
A pair multiplying to $-18$ and adding to $-3$ is $-6$ and $3$, so $x^2 - 3x - 18 = (x - 6)(x + 3)$. Swapping the signs gives $x^2 + 3x - 18$.
The products are $4x^2$, $10x$, $10x$ and $25$, giving $4x^2 + 20x + 25$; squaring each term alone misses the middle term $20x$.
$(3x - 2)^2 = (3x - 2)(3x - 2) = 9x^2 - 6x - 6x + 4 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4$; the constant is positive because $-2 \times -2 = 4$.
